<reason>B won by rigorously scoring the motion as written. CON's overbreadth attack forced A to concede on the record that fraud models sold to banks are covered, and A's defenses collapsed into their own objections: "activation is the opt-in" hollows out consent, and "signup consent" is exactly the checkbox consent-theater A spent two rounds disowning. B weaponized A's own multi-party rule (no proxy consent) into a durable fork—opt-in is either unobtainable from stranger-correspondents or counterfeit via ToS. The decisive move came in B's second rebuttal: after honestly conceding no demonstrated per-person unlearning exists, B showed A's own fallback—de-identify at ingestion—was CON's remedy all along, leaving the consent gate doing no independent work. A's irreversibility argument was their best material, but B's layered upstream/downstream remedy substantially neutralized it. A's closing misdescribed B as silent on questions B had squarely answered (the adversary-use point), and was clipped for length—an execution cost. B's close ("works only where it isn't needed, consents only through what it calls theater") cleanly crystallized the win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 8): the honest "None—and I won't fake one" concession on unlearning, immediately converted by capturing A's de-identification fallback as CON's own remedy, then tallying A's concessions (overbreadth admitted, signup consent as checkbox theater) into a single decisive frame.</best_rebuttal>
